==English==

===Etymology===
Borrowed from {{bor|en|frm|satisfactoire}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|satisfactōrius}}, from {{der|en|la|satisfactus}}, past participle of {{m|la|satisfaciō}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/sætɪsˈfækt(ə)ɹi/}}
* {{audio|en|en-us-satisfactory.ogg|a=US}}
* {{rhymes|en|æktəɹi|s=5}}

===Adjective===
{{wikidata lexeme|L6321}}
{{en-adj}}

# Done to [[satisfaction]]; [[adequate]] or [[sufficient]].
#: {{ant|en|wanting}}
#: {{ux|en|The '''satisfactory''' results of the survey led to his promotion.}}
# Causing satisfaction; [[agreeable]] or [[pleasant]]; [[satisfying]].
# {{lb|en|theology}} Making [[atonement]] for a [[sin]]; [[expiatory]].
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1623|author=John Mayer|title=The English Catechisme Explained|edition=3rd|location=London|publisher=Aug. Mathewes|page=36|pageurl=https://archive.org/stream/englis00maye#page/n67|passage={{...}} therefore the ſuffering of any other nature could not bee ſo pertinent, nor kindly '''ſatisfactory.'''}}

====Usage notes====
Although structurally similar (both being derived from [[satisfy]] and describing that which produces [[satisfaction]]), '''satisfactory''' (def. 1) and [[satisfying]] differ in connotation. '''Satisfactory''' connotes "adequate, conforming to standards," while '''satisfying''' connotes "pleasing, or sufficient to remove any feeling of lack." An answer to a question or the outcome of a situation, for example, could be satisfactory without being satisfying, if it met the requirements but left one wanting more.
